subtopic_detail: School exclusion period and notification for mumps in a vaccinated child
stem:
You are the resident in a regional emergency department. A 7-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with 3 days of fever and a tender swelling in front of and below both ears. He is finding it hard to open his mouth wide enough to eat.

His mother confirms from the immunisation record that he received two doses of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, the second at 18 months. The family returned 16 days ago from a holiday in Fiji, where an older cousin had a similar illness with facial swelling.

On examination the swelling obscures the angle of the jaw on both sides. The testes are normal in size and non-tender and there is no neck stiffness. A buccal swab has been collected for viral polymerase chain reaction and the result is pending. His mother asks when he can return to school.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral swelling obscuring the angle of the jaw, oral mucosa moist, no neck stiffness, testes normal
data_table.Investigations: Buccal swab for viral polymerase chain reaction pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about school exclusion and public health action?

options.text: Exclude until the facial swelling has completely resolved, and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Resolution of swelling can take 10 days or more and is not the criterion used in Australia; exclusion is tied to a fixed interval from swelling onset, not to clinical resolution. Notification is correct but the exclusion advice is not. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps

options.text: Exclude for 5 days from the onset of the facial swelling, and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Australian public health guidance sets exclusion at 5 days after the onset of parotid swelling, which covers the period of greatest viral shedding, and mumps is a notifiable condition in every state and territory. Two documented vaccine doses reduce but do not remove the risk of infection and transmission, so the exclusion period still applies. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps
NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.text: Exclude for 9 days from the onset of the facial swelling, and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Nine days reflects older international guidance based on the full duration of viral shedding; current Australian guidance shortened this to 5 days because transmission after that point is uncommon. (Source: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps)
source_refs: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps

options.text: Allow immediate return to school because he is vaccinated, and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Vaccine effectiveness against mumps after two doses is around 80 to 90 per cent and breakthrough cases shed virus, so vaccination status does not waive exclusion. This is the anti-pattern of treating an immunisation record as proof of non-infectivity. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Mumps)
source_refs: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Mumps

options.text: Exclude for 4 days from the onset of the fever, and notify the public health unit
options.rationale: Four days from fever onset is the measles exclusion rule applied to the wrong illness; the mumps clock starts at parotid swelling, which often begins after the prodromal fever. (Source: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)
source_refs: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

explanation.summary: Mumps remains in circulation in the Pacific and in under-immunised Australian communities, and breakthrough disease in twice-vaccinated children is well described. The public health response rests on three actions: laboratory confirmation by buccal swab polymerase chain reaction, exclusion from school or childcare, and notification so that contacts can be traced and vaccinated. Complications worth specifically examining for are orchitis in post-pubertal males, aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis and sensorineural hearing loss. Serology is a poor confirmatory test in the vaccinated because the immunoglobulin M response is often absent.
key_points: Exclusion is 5 days from onset of parotid swelling, not from fever onset and not until resolution
Mumps is notifiable in all Australian jurisdictions; notify on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for the swab result
Two vaccine doses give roughly 80 to 90 per cent protection, so breakthrough infection does not exclude the diagnosis
Buccal swab polymerase chain reaction is the confirmatory test of choice; immunoglobulin M serology is unreliable after vaccination
explanation.pearls: Collect the buccal swab within 3 days of parotid swelling onset if possible, since polymerase chain reaction sensitivity falls sharply beyond day 5 of swelling.

sources.label: CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Mumps
NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

subtopic_detail: Management of extensive molluscum contagiosum on a background of atopic dermatitis
stem:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her mother, who has counted about 30 small firm bumps with a dimple in the centre across the girl's trunk and both armpits. They appeared over 4 months and a few have become red and crusted in the last fortnight.

She has had eczema since infancy, currently managed with a moisturiser alone. Her mother is scratching at the bumps herself when bathing her, and wants them scraped off before the girl starts kindergarten in 6 weeks.

The girl has had no serious or recurrent infections, her growth has followed the 50th centile, and her immunisations are up to date. On examination there are dome-shaped pearly papules with dry, itchy, excoriated pink patches surrounding many of them. There is no cellulitis and she is systemically well.

data_table.Examination: About 30 dome-shaped umbilicated papules on trunk and axillae, surrounding dry excoriated pink patches, no spreading erythema or fluctuance
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile since birth

options.text: Refer for curettage of all lesions under general anaesthesia before she starts kindergarten
options.rationale: Curettage under general anaesthesia exposes a well child to anaesthetic risk and scarring for a self-limiting condition, and new lesions commonly appear afterwards from subclinical infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Apply liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to each lesion at fortnightly intervals until they clear
options.rationale: Cryotherapy is painful, poorly tolerated in preschoolers and risks post-inflammatory pigment change or scarring in a condition that resolves without treatment. It is the physical-destruction anti-pattern applied to a benign viral eruption. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Prescribe oral cephalexin for 7 days and exclude her from kindergarten until the lesions clear
options.rationale: There is no cellulitis or systemic illness, so antibiotics are not indicated; the crusting reflects the inflammatory host response rather than bacterial superinfection. Molluscum also carries no exclusion requirement in Australian childcare guidance. (Source: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services)
source_refs: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

options.text: Request lymphocyte subsets and immunoglobulins to investigate the extensive lesion count
options.rationale: Thirty lesions is within the ordinary range for a child with atopic dermatitis, whose impaired skin barrier allows wider spread; immune investigation is reserved for hundreds of lesions, facial confluence or other infection red flags, none of which are present here. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum

options.text: Treat the surrounding dermatitis with a topical corticosteroid and allow the lesions to resolve
options.rationale: Molluscum is self-limiting over 6 to 18 months, and the itch driving scratching and autoinoculation comes from the surrounding dermatitis, so controlling that eczema with a topical corticosteroid reduces spread and secondary infection. Active destruction adds pain and scarring without shortening the natural history. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum
Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection of the epidermis that resolves spontaneously, usually within 18 months, and the Australian paediatric position is to avoid destructive treatment in well children. Children with atopic dermatitis develop more numerous and more widespread lesions because barrier dysfunction and scratching spread the virus. A halo of dermatitis around lesions, sometimes called molluscum dermatitis, is common and responds to topical corticosteroid. Crusting, redness and swelling of individual lesions frequently signal the immune response that precedes resolution rather than bacterial infection. There is no requirement to exclude an affected child from childcare or school.
key_points: Lesions clear spontaneously over 6 to 18 months; destructive treatment adds pain and scarring without changing that course
Treating the surrounding eczema reduces scratching and therefore autoinoculation and spread
Inflamed crusted lesions usually herald immune-mediated resolution, not bacterial superinfection
No childcare or school exclusion is required in Australia; covering lesions under clothing is sufficient
Immune workup is reserved for hundreds of lesions, confluent facial disease or other infection red flags
explanation.pearls: The beginning-of-the-end sign is an individual molluscum becoming red, swollen and tender over about a week; it predicts clearance of that lesion and should not trigger antibiotics.

sources.label: NHMRC Staying Healthy: preventing infectious diseases in early childhood education and care services

subtopic_detail: Timing of factor replacement relative to imaging in a suspected joint bleed in severe haemophilia A
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on for the emergency department. A 6-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A, established on twice-weekly prophylaxis, is brought in 40 minutes after falling from a scooter onto his right arm.

He tells you his elbow feels tingly and full rather than painful, and he is holding it slightly bent and refusing to straighten it. His last prophylaxis dose was 3 days ago. He has no inhibitor on his most recent annual screen.

On examination the right elbow looks the same size as the left with no visible swelling or bruising, and the skin is not warm. He resists the last 20 degrees of extension. Distal pulses and sensation are normal. The emergency consultant asks whether you want a radiograph and an orthopaedic opinion first.

data_table.Examination: Right elbow held in slight flexion, no visible swelling or bruising, resists terminal extension, normal distal pulses and sensation
data_table.Treatment history: Twice-weekly factor VIII prophylaxis, last dose 3 days ago, no inhibitor on most recent annual screen

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give a factor VIII concentrate dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
options.rationale: The tingling, full sensation with loss of terminal extension is the earliest symptom of a joint bleed, and factor replacement must precede imaging or specialist review because every hour of delay increases the bleed volume and the risk of long-term arthropathy. Absence of visible swelling is expected this early and does not argue against a bleed. (Source: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia)
source_refs: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia
World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

options.text: Give a desmopressin dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
options.rationale: Desmopressin releases stored factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, which requires residual endogenous factor and therefore works only in mild haemophilia A or von Willebrand disease; a child with severe disease has no store to release. This is the classic near-pair with factor concentrate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Apply ice and a sling now, with review in 24 hours if the symptoms have not settled
options.rationale: Rest, ice, compression and elevation are useful adjuncts but never a substitute for factor replacement, and a 24-hour delay in a severe phenotype allows a substantial haemarthrosis to accumulate. (Source: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia)
source_refs: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia

options.text: Give an oral tranexamic acid dose now, before any imaging or orthopaedic assessment
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid stabilises clot that has already formed and has a genuine role in mucosal and dental bleeding, but it cannot generate thrombin in the absence of factor VIII and is not adequate monotherapy for a joint bleed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange a radiograph now, before deciding whether factor replacement is required
options.rationale: Plain radiographs do not show early haemarthrosis and cannot exclude one, so imaging that gates treatment simply delays it; a fracture can be excluded after factor has been given. (Source: World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia)
source_refs: World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

explanation.summary: Joint bleeding is the dominant cause of long-term disability in severe haemophilia, and the Australian treatment principle is that suspicion of a bleed is itself the indication for factor replacement. Children learn to recognise a prodromal aura of tingling or fullness before pain or swelling appears, and that report should be believed and acted on. Every haemophilia treatment centre issues families with an emergency plan directing that factor is given first and assessment follows. For a target joint or an established bleed, factor VIII is typically dosed to raise the plasma level to around 50 per cent, with repeat dosing guided by the treating centre. Inhibitor development changes the whole approach, which is why the inhibitor status is checked regularly.
key_points: Suspected bleed equals treat: factor replacement precedes imaging, orthopaedic review and analgesia decisions
Early haemarthrosis presents as tingling or fullness with loss of terminal range before any visible swelling
Desmopressin works only where residual endogenous factor VIII exists, so it has no role in severe haemophilia A
Tranexamic acid is an adjunct for mucosal bleeding, never monotherapy for a joint bleed
Contact the haemophilia treatment centre early, since dosing and repeat scheduling are centre-directed
explanation.pearls: Aim for a factor VIII level of about 50 per cent for a joint bleed and give the first dose within an hour of symptom onset; the roughly 12-hour half-life of factor VIII means repeat dosing is planned in 12-hourly cycles.

sources.label: Australian Haemophilia Centre Directors Organisation: Guidelines for the management of haemophilia in Australia
World Federation of Hemophilia Guidelines for the Management of Hemophilia

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing constitutional delay from pathological delayed puberty in a 14-year-old boy
stem:
A 14-year-old boy attends your general practice with his father, who is worried that his son is the shortest boy in his year and still looks like a child next to his friends. The boy is embarrassed and says he is teased in the change rooms.

He is otherwise well, with a normal appetite, no headaches, no visual symptoms and no anosmia. His bowels are regular and he has had no weight loss. He plays soccer twice a week. His father recalls being the shortest in his own class until he was 16 and then growing 25 cm.

On examination his height is on the 3rd centile, tracking along that line on the growth chart, with a growth velocity of 5 cm over the last year. Testicular volume is 5 mL bilaterally by orchidometer with early pubic hair. A bone age film reports a skeletal age of 12 years 6 months.

data_table.Growth: Height on the 3rd centile tracking along the same line, growth velocity 5 cm in the past 12 months, weight on the 10th centile
data_table.Examination: Testicular volume 5 mL bilaterally, early pubic hair, no anosmia, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 12 years 6 months at a chronological age of 14 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request luteinising hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, testosterone and a karyotype
options.rationale: Gonadotrophin and karyotype testing is indicated when puberty has not started by age 14 in a boy; here a testicular volume of 5 mL confirms that the axis has already activated, so these tests will simply return pubertal values. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty

options.text: Request coeliac serology, thyroid function and inflammatory markers looking for chronic disease
options.rationale: Screening for occult chronic disease is appropriate where growth velocity has fallen or weight has crossed centiles downwards; his velocity of 5 cm per year with stable centiles and a normal appetite argues against it. (Source: RCH CPG: Short stature)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Short stature

options.text: Reassure the family and review with repeat growth measurements in 6 months
options.rationale: Testicular volume of 5 mL means puberty has begun, a bone age delayed by about 20 months predicts continued growth after peers have finished, and the paternal history of a late growth spurt completes the picture of constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Serial growth measurement is both the diagnostic test and the management. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamic region
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is warranted with headache, visual field loss, anosmia suggesting Kallmann syndrome, or a falling growth velocity with absent pubertal signs; none of those features is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Delayed puberty

options.text: Start a short course of monthly intramuscular testosterone to induce the growth spurt
options.rationale: Low-dose testosterone priming is reserved for boys with significant psychosocial distress whose puberty has not yet started, and giving it once puberty is established risks accelerating bone age and reducing final adult height. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the commonest cause of short stature with delayed maturation in adolescent boys and is a diagnosis supported by positive findings rather than one of pure exclusion. The three supportive findings are a height tracking parallel to a centile line with a normal growth velocity, a bone age delayed relative to chronological age, and a family history of late maturation in a parent or sibling. Testicular volume is the single most informative examination finding: 4 mL or more means the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis has activated. The delayed bone age is reassuring because it represents growth potential still in hand. Psychosocial distress is real and deserves acknowledgement, follow-up and, where severe, endocrine referral for consideration of short-course testosterone priming.
key_points: Testicular volume of 4 mL or more confirms that puberty has started, whatever the height centile
Normal growth velocity with a height tracking along a centile line points away from chronic disease
A bone age delayed relative to chronological age represents retained growth potential and predicts a later but adequate spurt
Red flags that change the approach are anosmia, headache, visual field defect, falling velocity and weight loss
Serial six-monthly growth measurement is both the investigation and the management in constitutional delay
explanation.pearls: A growth velocity below 4 cm per year in mid-childhood is the threshold that should trigger investigation rather than observation, irrespective of how short the child is on the centile chart.

subtopic_detail: Preventive therapy for a young household contact of smear positive pulmonary tuberculosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing children referred by the tuberculosis control unit. A 3-year-old girl is brought in because her father was diagnosed 3 weeks ago with sputum smear positive pulmonary tuberculosis and is now on directly observed therapy. She shares a bedroom with her parents.

She has no cough, no fever and no night sweats. Her weight is on the 50th centile and has tracked there since her 12-month check. She was born overseas and received bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination at birth, and the scar is visible on her left shoulder.

Examination is unremarkable with clear chest auscultation and no lymphadenopathy. A tuberculin skin test read at 72 hours shows 12 mm of induration. Her chest radiograph is reported as normal with clear lung fields and no hilar lymphadenopathy. Her father asks what happens next for his daughter.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy, bacille Calmette-Guerin scar on left shoulder
data_table.Investigations: Tuberculin skin test 12 mm induration at 72 hours; chest radiograph normal with no hilar lymphadenopathy
data_table.Growth: Weight on the 50th centile, tracking since 12 months of age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start daily isoniazid for 9 months with monthly clinical review
options.rationale: She is a close household contact of a smear positive case with a tuberculin skin test above the 10 mm threshold and active disease excluded clinically and radiologically, which is the definition of latent infection requiring preventive therapy. Nine months of daily isoniazid is a standard Australian regimen in young children, in whom the risk of progression to disseminated or meningeal disease is highest. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Start daily isoniazid and rifampicin for 6 months with monthly clinical review
options.rationale: Combination regimens for latent infection run for 3 months, not 6, and a 6-month two-drug course is neither a preventive regimen nor adequate treatment for active disease. The near-pair to know is 3 months of daily rifampicin with isoniazid, which is an accepted alternative when a shorter course improves completion. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.text: Repeat the tuberculin skin test in 8 weeks before deciding on any therapy
options.rationale: Repeat testing at 8 weeks applies to a contact whose initial test was negative and who is within the window period; a test already at 12 mm needs no repetition and waiting exposes a 3-year-old to the period of greatest progression risk. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.text: Request an interferon gamma release assay before deciding on any therapy
options.rationale: An interferon gamma release assay is most useful for resolving whether a positive tuberculin skin test reflects prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination, but a 12 mm reading in a household contact of a smear positive case already exceeds the treatment threshold whatever the assay shows. Vaccination given in infancy rarely produces induration of this size a decade later. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays

options.text: Observe without therapy and repeat the chest radiograph in 6 months
options.rationale: Observation alone accepts a risk of progression that is around 5 to 10 per cent lifetime overall but front-loaded and much higher in the first 2 years for a child of this age, in whom disseminated disease and tuberculous meningitis are the feared outcomes. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

explanation.summary: Contact tracing around a smear positive index case is coordinated by the state tuberculosis control unit, and children under 5 are the highest priority group because their risk of progression to severe disease is greatest. The sequence is always the same: exclude active disease clinically and radiologically first, because treating active tuberculosis with a single drug generates resistance, then treat latent infection. Tuberculin skin test cut-offs in Australia are 5 mm for the immunosuppressed and for contacts in some jurisdictions, and 10 mm for most other groups. Prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination in infancy causes only modest and waning induration and should not be used to dismiss a strongly positive test in a close contact. Children under 5 who are close contacts may be started on preventive therapy even when the initial test is negative, then reassessed at 8 to 12 weeks.
key_points: Exclude active disease with history, examination and chest radiograph before starting single-drug preventive therapy
Daily isoniazid for 9 months is a standard Australian paediatric latent infection regimen; 3 months of rifampicin with isoniazid is the shorter alternative
A positive tuberculin skin test in a close contact should not be attributed to infant bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination
Children under 5 carry the highest risk of progression to miliary disease and tuberculous meningitis
Notification and contact management are led by the state or territory tuberculosis control unit
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine is not routinely needed with isoniazid in well-nourished Australian children, but should be added for exclusively breastfed infants, malnourished children and adolescents on other neuropathic drugs.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection
National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Position statement on interferon gamma release assays
